title: AI-Powered Drone Arm Color Verification Station
description: An intelligent quality control system that uses computer vision and AMR integration to automatically verify drone arm colors against production orders, eliminating sorting errors and ensuring accuracy.
benefits: 89% reduction in AMR dwell time at QC station
executive_summary: The KACST Industry 4.0 Capability Center deployed an automated quality control station that integrates with Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs). The system uses a custom-trained YOLOv8 computer vision model to detect and count colored drone arms delivered by an AMR, compares the count to the active production order, and automatically dispatches the AMR upon successful verification.

business_challenge.industry_context: In a fast-paced drone assembly line, ensuring that the correct components are routed to the correct assembly station is critical. Manual verification of parts like colored drone arms is prone to human error, especially during high-volume production or when multiple similar orders are processed sequentially.
specific_problems: Frequent mix-ups of drone arm colors, leading to incorrect kits being sent to the final assembly station
Significant labor time spent on manually counting and verifying components
Lack of an automated audit trail to confirm which parts were verified
Delays in dispatching AMRs from the QC station as operators had to manually trigger the next step

business_impact.financial_loss: SAR 220,000 annually from rework costs, wasted operator time, and production line stoppages

selection_criteria: Must achieve >99% accuracy in identifying and counting multi-class colored drone arms
Must seamlessly integrate with the existing AMR fleet via REST API
Must provide a real-time dashboard for monitoring the verification process
The system must be capable of running on low-power edge devices like a Raspberry Pi

technology_components.details: Custom-trained for multi-class drone arm color detection
Real-time visualization, controls, and status updates
Python requests to poll status and dispatch robots via REST API
Raspberry Pi 4 connected to USB webcam for image capture and processing

implementation_details.methodology: Agile methodology with core model development first, followed by dashboard and AMR integration deployed iteratively

objectives: train and validate the YOLOv8 model to >99% accuracy
Set up the Raspberry Pi station
develop and test AMR API communication
Deploy the Docker container to production

quantitative_metrics.metric: AMR Dwell Time at QC Station

qualitative_impacts: Dramatically increased operator confidence and trust in the production process
Created a fully automated, hands-off verification point in the production line
Provided a digital audit trail for every batch, improving traceability

technical_architecture.system_overview: Dockerized Streamlit application running on Raspberry Pi 4 at the edge. USB camera provides live video feed processed locally by YOLOv8 model. Communicates with AMR fleet over network via REST API calls.

architecture_components.components: Raspberry Pi 4, USB Webcam, LED Lighting
architecture_components.specifications: Device mounted at QC station overlooking AMR drop-off point
Contained within Docker image for portability
Handles GET requests for AMR status and POST requests for dispatch
Real-time dashboard accessible from any browser on factory network

security_measures: Isolated IoT network VLAN with restricted access to AMR control server
scalability_design: Self-contained Docker image allows rapid deployment to new QC stations

future_roadmap.description: Expand vision model to identify physical defects like cracks or print artifacts
future_roadmap.expected_benefit: Single consolidated QC station for both correctness and quality

future_roadmap.description: Integrate with factory MES to pull production orders dynamically
future_roadmap.expected_benefit: Increased production agility for custom on-the-fly configurations

lessons_learned.lesson: Good Data is More Important Than a Complex Model
lessons_learned.description: High-quality training data captured under realistic factory conditions enabled lightweight YOLOv8 to perform exceptionally
lessons_learned.recommendation: Invest 80% effort in data collection, cleaning, and augmentation

lessons_learned.description: Operator feedback led to simplified interface with larger status indicators and manual override
lessons_learned.recommendation: Treat end-users as key stakeholders throughout entire development process

title: ROS2-Based Autonomous Mobile Robot (AMR) Fleet for Factory Logistics
description: An intelligent, driverless transport system built on ROS2, using SLAM navigation and a centralized communication hub to autonomously move parts between manufacturing, quality control, and assembly stations.
executive_summary: The KACST Industry 4.0 Capability Center deployed a fleet of Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) to eliminate manual material handling. The AMRs are built on a ROS2 base for robust navigation and control, with a high-level Android system for task management. They navigate using SLAM technology powered by 360° LiDAR and obstacle avoidance sensors.

business_challenge.industry_context: In modern manufacturing, the time parts spend being manually moved between stations is non-value-added waste. This manual transport is often inefficient, prone to errors, a potential safety hazard, and a major source of production bottlenecks.
specific_problems: Significant operator time was wasted walking parts between stations
Production would often halt at one station while waiting for parts to be manually delivered
Risk of damage to sensitive components during manual transport
No digital traceability of material flow between workstations

business_impact.financial_loss: SAR 450,000 annually in lost productivity due to operator transit time and line stoppages

selection_criteria: The system must navigate a dynamic factory environment safely and autonomously
Must provide a simple, accessible API for integration with other systems
Navigation system must be based on robust, industry-standard platform like ROS2
Fleet must be centrally managed but capable of decentralized task execution

technology_components.details: Bottom-mounted for low-level obstacle and cliff detection
Raspberry Pi running Node-RED communicating with AMR REST APIs

implementation_details.methodology: Integration-first approach focusing on API communication layer in Node-RED to ensure reliable AMR calling and dispatch

objectives: Develop Node-RED workflows for calling AMRs
test high-volume transport scenarios and traffic management

qualitative_impacts: Transformed factory logistics from chaotic manual process to predictable automated system
Significantly improved operator safety by removing need to push heavy carts
Created fully traceable digital record of every material movement

technical_architecture.system_overview: Two-layer software stack: ROS2 for navigation/mapping/sensor fusion, Android for task management and REST API. Central Raspberry Pi with Node-RED acts as fleet dispatcher.

architecture_components.components: Mobile Chassis, 360° LiDAR, Proximity Sensors, Battery, Drive Motors
ROS2 (Navigation & Control), Android OS (Task Management), REST API Server
architecture_components.specifications: SLAM algorithm for localization within pre-generated map
Central communication hub between factory stations and AMR fleet API

security_measures: Dedicated encrypted Wi-Fi network with token-based API authentication
scalability_design: Easy fleet expansion by registering new robots with central dispatcher

future_roadmap.description: Enable AMRs to communicate with building infrastructure for multi-floor operation
future_roadmap.expected_benefit: Fully autonomous factory-wide logistics network capable of multi-floor operation

lessons_learned.description: Consumer-grade Wi-Fi insufficient due to signal reflections and interference in factory environment
lessons_learned.recommendation: Invest in professional wireless site survey and deploy robust networking hardware from start

lessons_learned.description: Created standardized library of commands in Node-RED that all systems use
lessons_learned.recommendation: Treat internal factory communication as formal API with clear, consistent commands

title: Vision-Assisted Packing Workstation
description: Camera-verified kitting with barcode and weight checks prevents packing errors and improves throughput
benefits: 85% reduction in returns due to packing errors
executive_summary: This use case implements a vision-assisted packing workstation that verifies every drone kit before sealing. An overhead camera with AI vision checks contents and orientation, barcode/RFID scanners validate item and variant, and an integrated weight scale confirms final kit mass. Pick-to-light guides the operator, while the workstation prints labels and logs traceability to MES/ERP.

business_challenge.industry_context: Packing errors (missing accessories, wrong variant, duplicates) drive costly returns, rework, and customer dissatisfaction. Manual checklists are inconsistent under high takt and frequent SKU changes, especially when accessory bundles differ by customer/order.
specific_problems: Missing or extra components due to manual verification
Wrong variant/label mix-ups across SKUs and customers
No automated, final go/no-go validation before sealing

business_impact.financial_loss: SAR 520,000 annually from returns, rework, expedited reshipments, and customer penalties

selection_criteria: Real-time camera verification against BOM/kit template
Dual validation via barcode/RFID and final weight check
Seamless MES/ERP/WMS integration with label and packing-slip printing

technology_components.details: AI vision model for presence/orientation checks
Rules engine with ERP/MES/WMS connectors and label printer

implementation_details.methodology: Agile deployment with pilot station, iterative model tuning, and phased rollout to all packing bays

objectives: capture images of all SKUs and accessories

qualitative_impacts: Improved operator confidence with guided steps

technical_architecture.system_overview: Camera-enabled packing cell with edge inference and rule validation (vision + barcode/RFID + weight) that gates label printing and box sealing. Events and images are logged to MES/ERP for full traceability.

architecture_components.components: Industrial camera, barcode/RFID scanners, bench scale, pick-to-light
architecture_components.specifications: Millisecond timestamping; scale resolution ≤1g; camera ≥5MP with controlled lighting

architecture_components.components: Vision inference service, rules engine, ERP/MES/WMS connectors, label service
architecture_components.specifications: Real-time go/no-go, SKU template matching, image archival with lot/serial

architecture_components.components: Operator HMI, supervisor dashboard, audit/traceability reports
architecture_components.specifications: Step-by-step UI, exception handling, photo proof on pass/fail

future_roadmap.description: Add 3D bin-packing to propose optimal box and dunnage
future_roadmap.expected_benefit: 12% packaging material savings and safer shipments

future_roadmap.description: Link customer returns to station photos and signals for root-cause analytics
future_roadmap.expected_benefit: Additional 30% reduction in recurring packing issues

lessons_learned.lesson: Golden Samples and Weight Windows Matter
lessons_learned.description: Precise master images and tight weight tolerances were critical to prevent false accepts
lessons_learned.recommendation: Maintain golden-sample images per SKU/revision and review weight windows when BOMs change

title: Cobot Palletizing Station for Packaged Drones
description: A collaborative robot (Cobot) with suction grippers automates the final end-of-line task, picking finished drone packages and stacking them onto a pallet for shipment.
executive_summary: The KACST Industry 4.0 Capability Center automated its final packaging step with a collaborative robot. After a drone is boxed and taped, it is placed on a pickup surface. A photoelectric sensor detects the box's presence and sends a signal to a Raspberry Pi. A Node-RED workflow then commands the Cobot, which uses a vacuum-powered suction gripper to pick up the box and place it in a pre-defined pattern on a shipping pallet, making it ready for logistics.

business_challenge.industry_context: The final stage of packaging and palletizing is a classic bottleneck in many production lines. This task is highly repetitive, physically demanding, and ergonomically hazardous for human operators, often leading to repetitive strain injuries and inconsistent stacking quality.
specific_problems: High risk of musculoskeletal injuries for operators performing repetitive lifting and twisting motions to stack boxes
The manual palletizing speed was the primary constraint on the entire production line's throughput
Inconsistent and unstable stacking of boxes on the pallet, leading to potential product damage during transit
High labor costs associated with a low-skill, physically demanding end-of-line task

business_impact.financial_loss: SAR 280,000 annually in costs related to operator injuries, production bottlenecks, and damaged goods from unstable pallets

selection_criteria: The solution must be safe for operators to work alongside without requiring a large safety fence (a collaborative robot)
The robot's end-of-arm-tool must be able to reliably grip cardboard boxes without causing damage
The system must be triggered automatically by the presence of a new box
Must integrate seamlessly into the existing factory control system built on Node-RED and Raspberry Pi

implementation_details.methodology: Safety-first agile approach. The core robotic pick-and-place task was programmed first. Then, the sensor integration and safety systems were layered on and rigorously tested before the system was allowed to run at full speed in production.

objectives: design and test the suction gripper
develop the Node-RED workflow to link the sensor to the robot
validate the Cobot's collaborative safety features

qualitative_impacts: Vastly improved workplace ergonomics and eliminated the primary source of back and shoulder injuries on the line
Created a stable, predictable, and paced end to the production line, allowing the upstream processes to run at a consistently higher speed
Operators were upskilled from manual labor to robot supervision and exception handling

technical_architecture.system_overview: The workflow is triggered when a finished drone package slides into a pickup nest, breaking the beam of a photoelectric sensor. The sensor sends a digital high signal to the GPIO pins of a Raspberry Pi. A Node-RED flow detects this input and sends a 'start cycle' command to the Cobot's controller via a TCP/IP socket. The Cobot, equipped with suction grippers, executes its pre-programmed routine to pick the box and place it on the pallet.

architecture_components.components: 6-axis Collaborative Robot, Suction Cup End-of-Arm Tooling, Pickup Nest
architecture_components.specifications: Cobot operates without a safety fence due to its inherent force-limiting safety features
Provides a simple binary signal to trigger the automation
Acts as the simple, low-cost brain of the work cell, translating the sensor input into a robot command

security_measures: The Cobot and Raspberry Pi are on an isolated control network, inaccessible from the main corporate LAN, to prevent unauthorized commands
scalability_design: The Node-RED flow and the robot's palletizing program can be easily modified with a graphical interface to accommodate different box sizes or stacking patterns

future_roadmap.description: Integrate the cell with the AMR fleet. An AMR will be tasked with automatically delivering empty pallets to the station and removing full pallets for transport to the shipping area.
future_roadmap.expected_benefit: Create a fully autonomous end-to-end process from final assembly to the shipping dock

lessons_learned.lesson: For Simple Tasks, Simple Triggers are Best
lessons_learned.description: We initially considered using a vision system to find the box. However, the combination of a simple mechanical nest and a cheap photoelectric sensor proved to be faster, more reliable, and a fraction of the cost for this specific task.
lessons_learned.recommendation: Don't over-engineer the solution. Always evaluate the simplest possible sensor and control strategy first; it's often the most robust.

lessons_learned.lesson: Collaborative Safety Requires a Risk Assessment
lessons_learned.description: While Cobots are inherently safer, they are not inherently safe. A formal risk assessment was still required to validate speeds, payload, and potential pinch points to ensure it was truly safe for operators to work alongside.
lessons_learned.recommendation: Always perform a thorough risk assessment when deploying any robot, even a collaborative one. Safety is a system property, not just a product feature.
